The 2nd Party-opposite parties have filed a (the main affidavit-in-opposition having not been filed at all) supplementary affidavit-in-opposition and stated that the case land fell into the saham of the father of the opposite parties in partition Suit No.2 of 1969 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was filed by the father of the opposite parties. The father of the opposite parties took separate possession in his saham through Court on 6.2.82. Thereafter, the said Amiruddin Dhali, father of the opposite parties, transferred the case land to the opposite party nos. 1-3, who are his sons, by registered Heba-bil-Ewaj dated 13.8.84. Since then the opposite parties are in normal and peaceful possession of the case land and they have also constructed a building on the case land. The 1st Party-petitioners in an effort to re-open the partition have started various proceedings. The 1st Party-petitioner No.1 putting himself up as a member of the Executive Committee of a mosque situated within the original joint land and separated by a registered Deed of Wall much before the old Partition Suit No.2 of 1969, filed Title Suit No. 35 of 1987 on 2.2.87 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for fresh partition of the original joint estate, seeking to void the old partition decree and making the said Amiruddin Dhali and his brother Ali Meah Dhali as parties to the suit. The defendant No. 1 Amiruddin Dhali has filed written statement in the new partition suit on 2.2.87. Thereafter, on 20.3.87 the plaintiffs of the new suit filed an application for temporary injunction for protecting the present state of possession in the suit land. The Court fixed 2.4.87 for hearing the said injunction matter. However, the 1st Party-Petitioner No. 1 has been repeatedly obtaining adjournment in the hearing of the injunction matter. 51 days after filing of the new partition suit, 25 days after the written statement was filed in the new suit and 3 days after filing the injunction petition in the new suit and suppressing all those facts the 1st Party-petitioners filed the present application under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Before filing of the present application under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the opposite party No. 1 filed an application to the Police Commissioner to make arrangements to prevent trouble on the case land on 31.1.87. Under orders of the Commissioner, Dhaka Metropolitan Police, ansars regiment was posted on the case land to maintain peace and tranquility. The ansars are protecting the land ever since. 

 13. We do not think that this submission has any legs to stand. The jurisdiction once validly acquired by the Magistrate acting under sub-section (1) of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure docs not cease until and unless the said proceeding drawn under sub-section (1) is cancelled under subsection (5) or the subject matter of the proceeding is finally disposed of under sub-section (6) declaring a party to be entitled to possession thereof. At any stage of the proceeding the Magistrate may come to the conclusion that there is no longer any case for continuing the inquiry. The apprehension of breach of peace which was the sine qua non for drawing up the proceeding may cease to exist, or it may be shown to the Magistrate not only by the party required to attend, but by any other person interested that no such dispute as aforesaid exists or has existed. The exercise of power under sub-section (5) is not dependent upon the result of inquiry under subsection (t). Sub-section (5) provides for u special case in which the parties to the proceedings and even third parties are given the right to show that no dispute exists or has existed. The party who moves the Magistrate or cancellation of the preliminary order under sub-section (5) has the liberty to produce evidence before the Magistrate. What is evidence deepens upon the facts and circumstances of each case That a dispute does not exist or has not existed or that there is no apprehension of breach of peace may be proved to the satisfaction of the Magistrate by production of a single piece of paper. It depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the present case the 2l1d party opposite parties not only filed a detailed written objection, but also tiled the copies of the registered Deed of Waqf, registered Deed of Heba-bil-Ewaj, decree with Commissioner's papers in Title Suit No.2 of 1969, writ of delivery of possession and various other papers including a police warrant for posting of ansars dated 31.1.87. It is on those materials that the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate decided by his order dated 12.4.87 that Lie preliminary order passed under sub-section I should not -be cancelled. The learned Magistrate was perfectly entitled to come to a decision on the basis of the written statement and the papers submitted by the 2nd parity opposite parties. On revision the learned Additional Sessions Judge has equally the jurisdiction to decide whether the learned Magistrate was correct in not cancelling the preliminary order on 12.4.87. When a Magistrate passes a preliminary order under sub-section (1), he has to exercise a subjective satisfaction with regard to the apprehension of breach of peace. But when he decides to cancel or not to cancel the preliminary order on being moved under sub-section (5), his satisfaction is no longer subjective. He is required to take an objective decision after going through the papers and documents of both sides. This subsequent decision under sub-section (5) is subject to scrutiny by the provisional Court on a wider ground than the Magistrate's order passed under sub-section (1). An order passed under sub-section (1) is passed on subjective satisfaction and a higher Court will not substitute its own satisfaction in place of the satisfaction of the Magistrate. But an order passed under sub-section (5) is based on objective satisfaction and it is open to wider challenge before the revisional Court. 

 "A case in which a civil Court is already seized with the subject-matter of dispute and has passed an order regulating possession thereof or a case in which a decree for possession has been granted or a permanent injunction granted restraining the opposites party from interfering with the possession of the decree-holder, falls outside the jurisdiction of a Magistrate under section 145 Cr.P.C. Action can of course be taken always under sections 107 and 151 of the Criminal Procedure Code to prevent breach of peace in case of this nature, but no order by a criminal Court for attachment of the property under section 145 Cr. P.C. can validly be made."
